侠
侠 · One Word, Loose in the World
A Map of Imaginations

Here's a word: 侠 (xiá) — someone who lives by their own code, fights for those who can't, and bows to no boss, no king, no law. No clean English exists: chivalry, bushidō, caballería all miss.

I handed it to people around the world — friends, teachers, strangers online, one scholar — told them almost nothing, and asked: what do you see?

  • an American painted Spider-Man swinging through a bamboo forest
  • a French participant flat-out refused AI — "no I'm not gonna use AI. I'm bad drawing but I'll try" — and drew a girl in red by hand
  • an Indian participant wrote a poem about refusing to let an AI do his thinking for him
  • a Brazilian participant asked Gemini to generate two hands reaching across the dark
  • a Taiwanese participant calmly traced the word back two thousand years to 司馬遷

Same word; a dozen different worlds. That's the idea: a concept doesn't break when it crosses a border — it gets reborn. Nobody got 侠 "wrong." This is a map of imaginations.

Insight
What the Map Shows
Across twelve participants, 侠 did not appear as one stable cultural object. Each person rebuilt it through their own world: Spider-Man in bamboo, a hand-drawn girl in red, a poem about refusing to let AI think for him, two hands reaching through darkness, a Taiwanese historical reading that traced the word back to 司馬遷. The map shows that cultural concepts do not simply survive translation by remaining pure; they survive because people keep remaking them.
What stayed recognizable was not a costume, gender, weapon, or nation, but a moral impulse: someone acts from an inner code when ordinary systems feel insufficient. That impulse can become justice, resistance, discipline, loyalty, longing, or self-cultivation depending on who receives it. So the map does not answer what 侠 is once and for all. It shows why people keep finding new reasons to recreate it.
Coda · A Field Note
The Master Who Says 侠 Is Gone

I met him at a martial-arts club in Waseda. 内海 (Uchimi) spent twenty years in China, trained under masters in Shanghai and Taiwan, and speaks fluent Chinese — he even helped edit the very books in these photographs. I asked him what 侠 meant, and instead he taught me how to stand, how to move, how to move the breath.

侠 is the one who helps the weak. Today the word has slid into a polite name for the underworld. In the old society the gangs and the martial arts were tightly bound — a theme you still meet in the movies. As the times changed, so did the standing of 侠: the role of the state grew vast, ordinary life stopped running on mutual aid, dire poverty thinned out, and no one trades in lives through martial skill anymore. The idea of 侠 is gone now. We can only miss it — or enjoy it — on the screen.

— 内海, by message, after class
Where I Land

I should be honest about where this project started. I began it half-believing that the people who guard a tradition most fiercely are the ones holding it back — that the future of 侠 belonged to the young people remaking it, and that the old masters were simply too stubborn to let it change. I wanted to show how a concept travels, and how much imagination this generation brings to something ancient.

Meeting him complicated that. He is, by his own account, pessimistic — he believes 侠 is gone. And yet at the club he teaches beginners patiently, without any airs, never demanding that anyone grasp the deeper meaning before they are ready. What I saw was not a gatekeeper. It was someone who has loved one culture his whole life, faithfully, from beginning to end, and stayed humble about it. That kind of devotion is its own argument — one I hadn't accounted for.

So I find myself holding two things at once. I still believe what this gallery shows: that a concept survives by being reimagined, that its flexibility is what lets it cross borders and generations. But he made me feel the weight of the other side — how much is carried in the original, and how much love and labor it takes to keep it intact, not only alive in new forms. I don't think transformation and preservation have to be enemies. But I won't pretend I've resolved them. Maybe it's a question with no clean answer; maybe it's one that only gets worked out slowly, by many people, over time. For now I'd rather leave it open than close it too early.
